source_text: Longum est ire per singula: nihil in homine membrorum est, quod non et necessitatis causa sit, et decoris: et quod magis mirum est, eadem figura omnibus, sed quaedam unicuique lineamenta deflexa. Sic et similes universi videmur, et inter se singulis dissimiles invenimur. Quid nascendi ratio? Quid cupido generandi? Nonne a Deo data est? et ut ubera partu maturescente lactescant, et ut tener foelus ubertate lactei roris adolescat? Nec universitati solummodo Deus, sed et partibus consulit. Britannia sole deficitur, sed circumfluentis maris tepore recreatur: Aegypti siccitatem temperat Nilus amnis: colit Euphrates Mesopotamiam: pro imbribus pensat Indus, et serere Orientem dicitur et rigare. Quod si ingressus aliquam domum, omnia exculta, disposita, ornata vidisses, utique praeesse ei crederes dominum, et illis bonis rebus multo esse meliorem: ita in hac mundi domo, cum coelum terramque perspicias, providentiam, ordinem, legem, crede esse universitatis dominum parentemque ipsis sideribus et totius mundi partibus pulchriorem. Ni forte, quoniam de providentia nulla dubitatio est, inquirendum putas, utrum unius imperio, an arbitrio plurimorum coeleste regnum gubernetur: quod ipsum non est multi laboris aperire cogitanti imperia terrena, quibus exempla utique de coelo: quando umquam regni societas aut cum fide coepit, aut sine cruore discessit? Omitto Persas, de equorum hinnitu augurantes principatum; et Thebanorum permortuam fabulam, transeo: ob pastorum et casae regnum de geminis memoria notissima est; generi et soceri bella toto orbe diffusa sunt: et tam magni imperii duos fortuna non cepit. Vide caetera: rex unus apibus, dux unus gregibus, in armentis rector unus: tu in coelo summam potestatem dividi credas, et scindi veri illius ac divini imperii totam potestatem? cum palam sit parentem omnium Deum nec principium habere, nec terminum; qui nativitatem24 omnibus praestet, sibi perpetuitatem, qui ante mundum fuerit sibi ipse pro mundo; qui universa, quaecumque sunt, verbo jubet, ratione dispensat, virtute consummat. Hic nec videri potest, visu clarior est; nec comprehendi, tactu purior est; nec aestimari, sensibus major est, infinitus, immensus, et soli sibi, tantus quantus est, notus; nobis vero ad intellectum pectus angustum est; et ideo sic eum digne aestimamus dum inaestimabilem dicimus. Eloquar quemadmodum sentio; magnitudinem Dei qui se putat nosse, minuit; qui non vult minuere, non novit. Nec nomen Deo quaeras, Deus nomen est. Illic vocabulis opus est cum per singulos propriis appellationum insignibus multitudo dirimenda est: Deo, qui solus est, Dei vocabulum totum est. Quem si patrem dixero, terrenum opineris; si regem, carnalem suspiceris; si dominum, intelliges utique mortalem. Aufer additamenta nominum, et perspicies ejus claritatem. Quid? quod omnium de isto habeo consensum: audio vulgus, quum ad coelum manus tendunt, nihil aliud quam DEUM dicunt; et, DEUS MAGNUS EST; et, DEUS VERUS EST, et, SI DEUS DEDERIT. Vulgi iste naturalis sermo est, an Christiani confitentis oratio? et qui Jovem principem volunt, falluntur in nomine, sed de una potestate consentiunt.
pass_a_gloss: It is long to go through individual things: there is nothing in man of members, which is not both for the cause of necessity and of decoration: and what is more wonderful, the same figure for all, but certain lineaments are deflected for each one. Thus we seem similar to all, and among themselves individually we are found dissimilar. What is the reason of birth? What is the desire of generating? Is it not given by God? And so that breasts with parturition maturing become milky, and so that the tender foal with the abundance of milky dew grows up? Nor does God consult for the universe alone, but also for the parts. Britain is deficient in sun, but is restored by the warmth of the surrounding sea: the Nile river tempers the dryness of Egypt: the Euphrates cultivates Mesopotamia: the Indus compensates for the rains, and is said to sow and to irrigate the East. But if you had entered some house, and had seen all things cultivated, arranged, adorned, you would certainly believe that a master is in charge of it, and that he is much better than those good things: so in this house of the world, when you look at the heaven and the earth, believe that there is a master and parent of the universe, and one more beautiful than the stars themselves and the parts of the whole world. Unless perhaps, since there is no doubt about providence, you think that it should be investigated, whether the heavenly kingdom is governed by the command of one, or by the decision of many: which itself is not much labor to reveal to one who thinks, by means of earthly empires, of which the examples are certainly from heaven: when did the society of a kingdom ever begin with faith, or end without bloodshed? I pass over the Persians, who take the neighing of horses as an omen of principality; and the utterly dead fable of the Thebans, I skip: the memory of the kingdom of the shepherds and the hut is most well-known on account of the twins: wars between son-in-law and father-in-law have been spread throughout the whole world: and fortune has not captured two such great empires. See the rest: one king for the bees, one leader for the flocks, one ruler for the herds: do you believe that the highest power is divided in heaven, and that the whole power of that true and divine empire is torn apart? When it is clear that God, the parent of all, has neither beginning nor end; who provides birth for all, perpetuity for himself, who was before the world for himself as the world; who commands all things, whatever they are, by his word, dispenses by his reason, completes by his power. This one cannot be seen, is clearer than sight; cannot be comprehended, is purer than touch; cannot be estimated, is greater than the senses, infinite, immeasurable, and known only to himself, so great as he is; for us, indeed, the breast is narrow for understanding; and therefore we esteem him worthily when we say that he is inestimable. I will speak as I feel; whoever thinks that he knows the magnitude of God, diminishes it; whoever does not want to diminish it, does not know it. Nor should you seek a name for God, God is a name. There, words are necessary when a multitude must be distinguished by individual proper insignia of appellations: for God, who is alone, the whole word God is sufficient. If I call him Father, you will think him earthly; if King, you will suspect him to be carnal; if Lord, you will understand him to be mortal. Remove the additions of names, and you will perceive his clarity. What? Since I have consensus from all about this: I hear the common people, when they stretch out their hands to heaven, say nothing other than GOD; and, GOD IS GREAT; and, GOD IS TRUE; and, IF GOD GIVES. Is this the natural speech of the common people, or the confession of a Christian? And those who want Jupiter to be the prince, are deceived in the name, but consent to one power.

pass_b_english: Covering every detail would take too long: no part of the human body exists without serving both necessity and beauty, and what is even more remarkable, all of us share the same basic form while each individual bears distinct features. Thus we appear alike as a species, yet we are found to be unlike one another as individuals. What drives birth? What fuels the desire to procreate? Are these not gifts from God? He makes the breasts swell with milk as childbirth approaches, and he lets the newborn infant thrive on that milky abundance. God does not provide for the whole alone; he cares for the parts as well. Britain lacks sun, yet the encircling sea warms it; the Nile softens Egypt's aridity; the Euphrates cultivates Mesopotamia; the Indus makes up for absent rain, sowing and watering the East. If you entered a house and found everything tilled, ordered, and adorned, you would certainly conclude that a master runs it—one far superior to the good things within. So it is with this house of the world: when you survey heaven and earth, recognize a master and father of the universe, one more beautiful than the stars themselves and all the world's parts. Unless, since providence is beyond doubt, you think we must investigate whether the heavenly kingdom is governed by the command of one or by the will of many—a question that demands little thought from anyone who considers earthly empires, whose patterns certainly come from heaven. When has a partnership of rule ever begun in good faith or ended without bloodshed? I pass over the Persians, who read princely omens from the neighing of horses, and I skip the long-dead fable of the Thebans; the story of the twins and their shepherd's-hut kingdom is etched in memory, and wars between son-in-law and father-in-law have spread across the whole world, yet fortune has not seized two such great empires. Look at the rest: one king for the bees, one leader for the flocks, one ruler for the herds—do you really believe that supreme power is divided in heaven, that the whole authority of that true and divine empire is torn apart? It is clear that God, the parent of all, has neither beginning nor end; he grants birth to all things, perpetuity to himself, existing before the world for himself as the world's cause; he commands all things by his word, governs them by his reason, completes them by his power. He cannot be seen, yet he is clearer than sight; he cannot be grasped, yet he is purer than touch; he cannot be measured, yet he surpasses the senses—infinite, immeasurable, known only to himself, as great as he is. Our hearts are too narrow to comprehend him, and so we honor him worthily only when we call him inestimable. I speak as I perceive: whoever thinks he knows God's magnitude diminishes it; whoever refuses to diminish it does not know it. Do not seek a name for God—God is the name. Among mortals, words are necessary to distinguish a multitude by individual titles; for God, who is alone, the single word "God" suffices. If I call him Father, you picture an earthly one; if King, you suspect a fleshly ruler; if Lord, you understand a mortal master. Strip away the added titles, and you will perceive his brilliance. Consider the universal consensus on this point: I hear the common crowd, when they lift their hands to heaven, utter nothing but "GOD"; and "GOD IS GREAT"; and "GOD IS TRUE"; and "IF GOD GIVES." Is this the natural speech of the multitude, or the confession of a Christian? And those who wish to make Jupiter the supreme ruler are deceived in the name, yet they agree on a single power.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Latin text. Pass A provides a literal gloss, while Pass B provides a fluent rendering. Both correctly handle the complex theological and philosophical arguments regarding God's nature and the order of the universe. The translation of 'pectus angustum est' as 'the breast is narrow' (Pass A) and 'our hearts are too narrow' (Pass B) both respect the Latin metaphor for the capacity of the human soul/intellect. The distinction between 'Deus nomen est' (God is a name) is preserved. All clauses, including the geographical examples and the historical/mythological references, are accounted for.
